newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea ruling party blasts opposition over labour row.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea ruling party blasts opposition over labour row.

text.p: South Korea's ruling New Korea Party blasted the opposition on Thursday for rejecting an offer to reopen debate on a controversial labour law which has prompted more than three weeks of industrial strife.
It said the opposition's rejection of the offer was "shameless behaviour".
"The opposition should agree to the talks that our party proposed," a party statement said.
Police also released a South Korean union leader who had been arrested for obstructing business by leading strikes, a prosecution official said on Thursday.
But four other unionists are still being held,

The prosecution official said Kim Im-shik, a union leader from Hyundai Heavy Industries in the southeast city of Ulsan, was released overnight after reqesting a review of the legality of his arrest. He was picked up on Saturday.

The move follows President Kim Young-sam's order to suspend execution of arrest warrants, issued to 20 leaders of the Korean Confederation of Trade Unions for organising more than three weeks of wildcat strikes against the controversial law, which allows companies to dismiss workers and replace strikers.
As part of a concession to the opposition, Kim agreed on Tuesday to send the law back to parliament for debate after conceding it had caused public anxiety and hurt the economy.
But opposition parties rejected Kim's offer on Wednesday saying any debate in parliament would be held only on condition the law was first revoked.

The four unionists, all from a shipyard run by Halla Heavy Industries, had not requested a similar review made by Kim Im-shik, pending a decision by prosecutors on whether charges relating to their arrest should be dropped, the prosecution official said.
He also said prosecutors would soon decide on whether to drop outstanding arrest warrants for 15 other leaders of the outlawed confederation.

The ruling party statement said President Kim's concession revise the law, which was rammed through parliament during a dawn session on December 26, removed grounds for any opposition or union resistance.

"It is really shameless behaviour...for the opposition to demand the nullification of the law, while it could not provide an alternative and has not put forward its own draft," said the statement, signed by spokesman Kim Chul.

On Wednesday, police allowed confederation boss Kwon Young-kil to lead a protest march through Seoul streets after he left Myongdong Cathedral where he had been sheltering from arrest. Kwon later returned to the church.
Spokesman Kim said it was wrong for the confederation to use the cathedral as its protest headquarters since arrest warrants had been suspended and police had withdrawn from the area.
President Kim, who argues the law would free up the labour market and trim company costs as well as boost competitiveness, has said dumping the legislation would go against the constitution.
Until his stunning about-face, he had refused even to meet opposition leaders to discuss the law.
His sudden reversal on Tuesday followed a decision by the confederation to call off indefinite work stoppages and limit industrial action to one day each week on Wednesdays.
